title: Norse Atlantic's Norwegian Arm Files for Bankruptcy as Lessors Terminate All 787 Leases
excerpt: Flights have been suspended since November 26; the parent company and UK subsidiary sit outside the filing while the airline contests the termination of leases on its 12 Dreamliners.
body:
• Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating subsidiary is filing for bankruptcy at the Agder District Court after lessors terminated the leases on all 12 of its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners.
  • All Norse flights have been suspended since Thursday, November 26; the listed parent, Norse Atlantic ASA, and the UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are seeking a way to keep part of the business operating.
  • The airline contests the validity of the termination notices from AerCap and BOC Aviation, which each own six of the aircraft.
  • If you hold a Norse booking, the operation that was to fly it has stopped flying; the UK subsidiary's position is the part of the group still being worked on, and no restart timetable has been announced.

Norse Atlantic Airways' Norwegian operating subsidiary is filing for bankruptcy after the airline failed to secure sufficient emergency financing, the company announced on Friday, hours after confirming that lessors had terminated the leases covering its entire fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. The filing, to the Agder District Court in Norway, follows Thursday's suspension of all flights and ends the scheduled operation four and a half years after the airline's launch.

"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations."

— Eivind Roald, CEO, Norse Atlantic

The fleet is the fight

Norse owned none of its aircraft. It leased six 787-9s from AerCap, on terms of about 12 years, and six from BOC Aviation, on terms of about 16 years, in agreements dating from 2021, according to Air Data News. Seven of the jets are registered in Norway and five in the United Kingdom under Norse Atlantic UK, which began operations in March 2023; all five British-registered aircraft were listed as parked as of November 25. Termination of the leases does not by itself mean the lessors have recovered the aircraft, and Norse has disclosed no timetable for their return. The airline "contests the validity of the termination notices," it said in a statement reported by Simple Flying.

How the numbers turned

Norse had been closing on profitability: its annual net loss narrowed from $135.5 million in 2024 to $61.9 million in 2025. In 2026 the trend reversed sharply. First-half net loss widened to $94.6 million from $20.8 million a year earlier, on income down 10.8% to $292.3 million, with technical maintenance costs up 30.1% and net financial expenses up 177%, including a $32.9 million noncash charge tied to a bond conversion. The airline had no fuel hedging in place as jet fuel prices rose, and it cut its own-network capacity by 64% in the second quarter without cutting its fuel bill proportionately.

The pivot that ran out of money

Norse launched in June 2022 between Oslo and New York, stepping into the long-haul gap Norwegian had left. The low-cost transatlantic model never held: between the summers of 2025 and 2026 the airline cut US capacity by more than 60%, withdrawing all Los Angeles services, until London Gatwick-Orlando was its sole remaining scheduled US route. Flying for other airlines grew from 11% of its flights in the second quarter of 2025 to 56% a year later, but the model concentrated risk — five Dreamliners returned when the six-aircraft IndiGo arrangement ended on November 1, and a smaller wet-lease deal with Pakistan International Airlines was disrupted by the suspension.

Already booked?

  • All Norse Atlantic flights have been suspended since November 26, 2026, and the Norwegian operating subsidiary is filing for bankruptcy — do not plan travel around a restart; none has been announced.
  • The bankruptcy filing covers the Norwegian subsidiary only. The listed parent and Norse Atlantic UK are not included, and management says it is working on a solution for the remaining business.
  • The airline contests the lease terminations on all 12 aircraft, so the fleet's future — and any resumption under the UK operation — remains undecided.

What happens next turns on two negotiations: whether AerCap and BOC Aviation's terminations stand, and whether the parent and UK subsidiary can assemble financing around whatever operation remains. Twelve nearly-new 787-9s, in a market short of widebodies, will not stay parked for long — the open question is whose colours they fly in.
